title: Joshua 14:6–15
context: Before Judah’s allotment, Caleb asks Joshua for the inheritance Moses promised him forty-five years earlier at Kadesh Barnea, when he and Joshua alone brought a faithful report about the land. Now eighty-five and still strong, Caleb requests the hill country of the Anakim, and Joshua gives him Hebron. The narrator twice notes that Caleb ‘wholly followed’ the LORD. Arminian and Reformed readers share this passage as a picture of faith and of God’s faithfulness to his word.

verses.text: Then the children of Judah came near to Joshua in Gilgal. Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, “You know the thing that the LORD spoke to Moses the man of God concerning me and concerning you in Kadesh Barnea.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people of Judah come to Joshua at Gilgal, and Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite reminds him of what God said at Kadesh Barnea. Some readers take ‘Kenizzite’ to suggest a family that joined Judah, though this is debated.

Arminian readers see Caleb appealing to God’s word, not his own merit.
verses.reformedNotes:
Caleb recalls the episode of the spies in Numbers 13–14. Joshua shared that experience.

Reformed readers see Caleb grounding his request in God’s promise. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faith resting on what God has said.

verses.text: I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh Barnea to spy out the land. I brought him word again as it was in my heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
Caleb was forty when Moses sent him to spy out the land, and he reported ‘as it was in my heart.’ His report was honest and believing.

Arminian readers see integrity and trust joined in Caleb’s response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Caleb spoke what he truly believed, not what was popular. His report rested on God’s promise rather than on the strength of the enemy.

Reformed readers see faith expressed in truthful testimony. Both traditions share this reading of Caleb as an example of courageous faith.

verses.text: Nevertheless, my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; but I wholly followed the LORD my God.
verses.arminianNotes:
The other spies made the people’s hearts melt, but Caleb ‘wholly followed the LORD my God.’ The contrast is sharp.

Arminian readers see wholehearted devotion as a real, responsive choice, set against the fear that spread through Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘Wholly followed’ describes undivided loyalty. Numbers 14:24 uses similar language of Caleb.

Reformed readers see such faithfulness as the fruit of God’s grace, often noting that Numbers 14:24 says Caleb ‘had another spirit with him.’ Both traditions agree that Caleb is presented as a model of faith.

verses.text: Moses swore on that day, saying, ‘Surely the land where you walked shall be an inheritance to you and to your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses swore that the land where Caleb walked would be his and his children’s, because he wholly followed the LORD. The promise is personal.

Arminian readers see God honoring faithful obedience with a promised inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Caleb’s inheritance rests on Moses’ oath, echoing Numbers 14:24 and Deuteronomy 1:36. The promise extends to his descendants.

Reformed readers see God freely rewarding the faith he produces. Both traditions agree that the reward is God’s gift and read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “Now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, as he spoke, these forty-five years, from the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. Now, behold, I am eighty-five years old, today.
verses.arminianNotes:
God has kept Caleb alive forty-five years since that promise; he is now eighty-five. God’s faithfulness is measured in years.

Arminian readers see God sustaining a faithful servant through the long wilderness period. The figures help readers estimate the length of the conquest, though the calculation is approximate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Caleb attributes his survival to God: ‘the LORD has kept me alive, as he spoke.’

Reformed readers see God’s providence preserving his servant to see the promise fulfilled. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s faithfulness over time.

verses.text: As yet I am as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me. As my strength was then, even so is my strength now for war, to go out and to come in.
verses.arminianNotes:
Caleb says he is as strong now as when Moses sent him, ready for war. His vigor is a sign of God’s care.

Arminian readers see Caleb’s readiness to keep acting in faith even in old age.
verses.reformedNotes:
Caleb’s strength is presented as God’s gift. He does not boast of his own ability but of what God has preserved.

Reformed readers see God equipping his servants for the tasks he gives. Both traditions read this as shared ground, encouraging faithfulness at every stage of life.

verses.text: Now therefore give me this hill country, of which the LORD spoke in that day; for you heard in that day how the Anakim were there, and great and fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out, as the LORD said.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Caleb asks for the hill country God promised, where the Anakim lived in fortified cities. “It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out.”

Arminian readers see humble faith: Caleb chooses the hardest task and trusts God for the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes:
Caleb asks for the very region that frightened the spies. His ‘it may be’ expresses dependence rather than doubt.

Reformed readers see faith that relies on God’s word, not human strength. Both traditions share this reading of Caleb’s confident yet humble request.

verses.text: Joshua blessed him; and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua blesses Caleb and gives him Hebron as an inheritance. The promise is fulfilled.

Arminian readers see faithful leaders honoring God’s word to a faithful servant. Joshua’s blessing confirms what God had promised long before.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joshua, the other faithful spy, grants Caleb’s request. Hebron was associated with Abraham (Genesis 13:18; 23:2).

Reformed readers see continuity between the patriarchs and the conquest. Both traditions read this as shared ground; Judges 1:20 and Joshua 15:13–14 describe Caleb taking Hebron.

verses.text: Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he followed the LORD, the God of Israel wholeheartedly.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hebron became Caleb’s inheritance ‘to this day’ because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly. The narrator repeats the reason.

Arminian readers see lasting blessing connected with wholehearted faith. Caleb’s choices at Kadesh still shape his family’s future.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator confirms the outcome and its reason. ‘Wholeheartedly’ echoes verses 8 and 9.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to his promise as the deeper cause behind Caleb’s reward. Both traditions agree on this verse and hold faith and God’s faithfulness together as shared ground.

verses.text: Now the name of Hebron before was Kiriath Arba, after the greatest man among the Anakim. Then the land had rest from war.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hebron was formerly called Kiriath Arba, after the greatest man among the Anakim. Then the land had rest from war.

Arminian readers see a pause in conflict after faithful action, echoing Joshua 11:23.
verses.reformedNotes:
The old name recalls the Anakim who once intimidated Israel. Their stronghold now belongs to a faithful Israelite.

Reformed readers see God giving rest as he promised. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with Hebrews 4 later reflecting on the deeper rest God offers.
